chunks: I2C address and data frames. The question: Explain address/data frames.
Everything on an I2C bus is built from 9-clock units: 8 bits plus one acknowledge bit. The first byte after START is the address frame.
It holds the 7-bit address of the chip and one bit saying read or write, and the chip that matches answers with an ACK. Every later byte is a data frame. Bytes go on until STOP.
Think of a delivery handed over in stages. The first item is the label: which house it is for, and whether you are delivering or collecting.
Every item after that is parcel contents. At each handoff, the receiver says "thanks" with one extra beat, the acknowledge. The bus fixes the label's meaning.
The contents are private between sender and house, and nothing says how many items remain.
A write to address 0x50 with data 0xA5. Read the SDA row left to right: the bits after START are 1010000 (0x50), then 0 for write, then the target pulls SDA low for the ACK.
The next eight bits, 10100101, are the data byte 0xA5, and the target ACKs again. SDA changes only while SCL is low.
Address frame: the first byte after START, with the 7-bit address and the read/write bit. Data frame: any later byte, 8 data bits followed by an acknowledge bit.
MSB first: the most significant bit (the leftmost, worth the most) goes out first. Read/write bit: the lowest bit of the address byte.
0 means the controller writes and 1 means it reads.
7-bit vs 8-bit notation: a datasheet may quote the address byte as sent on the wire, such as 0x90, instead of the 7-bit address, 0x48.
Register pointer: by habit, the first data byte after a write address picks a register inside the chip.
A chip has 7-bit address 0x48 (hexadecimal), which is 1001000 in binary.
The byte on the wire is the address shifted left one place (which doubles it), with the read/write bit added at the end. That gives 0x90 for a write and 0x91 for a read.
A datasheet that says "0x90" is quoting the wire byte. Give a software library 0x48. One address frame plus three data frames is 4 frames of 9 clocks, 36 clock ticks.
That is the whole idea.
"Each frame is nine clocks.
The address frame is 7 address bits MSB first plus a read/write bit, with the target pulling SDA low on the ninth clock to ACK; address 0x48 becomes 0x90 for a write and 0x91 for a read.
Data frames are 8 bits MSB first plus an ACK, driven by the controller on a write and by the target on a read. There's no length field: bytes continue until STOP.
What the bytes mean, such as a register pointer, is defined by the target."
